book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

chapters.file: ch27 - 15. Good Citizen Deadpool.md
chapters.relation: Using Aristotle's Politics, the chapter splits the good man from the good citizen and argues that the Marvel Universe's 'city' needs mercenaries to keep its balance between heroes and villains, as in Deadpool vs Thanos where the In-Betweener steps in when Death is imprisoned and the balance tips toward Chaos. Deadpool's contract killing - hitting Hydra and AIM targets heroes won't touch - fulfills his role in that city, so he can be a good citizen without being a good man, a standard of all-around virtue that Colossus, the 'boy scout' produced by CGI, better fits. The thought experiment of an assassin for 'Deadpooltopia' shows how a dreadful man can still be a good citizen by serving his city's own idea of the good.

chapters.file: ch28 - 16. The Beautiful Face Behind the Mask.md
chapters.relation: Reading Deadpool through Levinas's Totality and Infinity, the chapter treats his mask and nonstop jokes as the closed totality of an isolated 'I,' and his face-to-face encounters - Siryn touching his scarred head, Vanessa and Mercedes seeing and accepting his face, the dead-shark dialogue, the North Korean clones who share his DNA - as the epiphany of the other that grounds ethics. Levinas's account of murder as denying the other's face explains why Theresa (Siryn) stops Wade from executing Dr. Killebrew, the Weapon X torturer whose eyes showed he regarded Wade as meat. The chapter concludes that Deadpool's face is beautiful as the expression of his inner self, and that living for others rather than for his own (impossible) death is the ethical path he keeps glimpsing.

chapters.file: ch29 - 17. Wade Wilson Fights Like a Girl.md
chapters.relation: Staged as a Socratic dialogue in a professor's office, the chapter tests Peter Coogan's definition of the superhero (mission, powers, identity) against the Deadpool movie and finds Wade qualifies while mocking the genre. It then argues the film subverts the superhero genre's sexist conventions: Vanessa refuses the damsel role by grabbing the bar mercenary's crotch and later skewering Francis herself, Angel Dust knocks Colossus out, and Negasonic Teenage Warhead is 'a damsel to the rescue.' Applying Laura Mulvey's male gaze, it shows the camera lingering on Deadpool's body and adopting Vanessa's viewpoint in the Calendar Girl scene, with the Women in Refrigerators trope, Gwen Stacy's death, and the Hawkeye Initiative as evidence of what the movie overturns.

chapters.file: ch30 - V. Really Was That Necessary Why We Would Like to Apologize to Mr. Reynolds Who Really Is Trying the Best He C.md
ch31 - 18. Thus Slaughtered Deadpool.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues Deadpool is neither hero nor anti-hero but Nietzsche's Ubermensch beyond good and evil: perceiving the writers as the 'man at the typewriter' who keeps the Marvel cast as unwitting sheep under a slave morality, he kills the Marvel Universe in Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe to free them from their creators. In Deadpool Killustrated he murders the literary archetypes (Moby-Dick, the Little Mermaid, Tom Sawyer) so the heroes they inspired can never be written, compared to the Overman demolishing inherited values before they corrupt the next generation, and in Deadpool Kills Deadpool he slaughters every version of himself to force the creator-god into the open. Since 'good' and 'bad' are categories of the herd whose very source is corrupt, the author declines to judge the slaughter at all.

chapters.file: ch32 - 19. Deadpool Can’t Know Fear.md
chapters.relation: Borrowing Socrates' definition of courage as remaining steadfast in the face of danger and choosing death above dishonor, the chapter argues that Deadpool's healing factor removes his risk of death, so he cannot experience the fear of helpless annihilation, cannot display courage, and is not an anti-hero but 'post-heroic.' Worse, mapping Luttwak's post-heroic warfare of drones and ballistic missiles onto his invulnerability, the chapter shows how fighting Deadpool drags opponents like the ULTIMATUM contract army and Crossbones into a trap where they can never test his courage and are stripped of their role as defenders, becoming mere targets. It closes that having a little fear and the chance to overcome it might be better than being unable to die.

chapters.file: ch33 - 20. Deadpool’s Genocide of the Marvel Universe.md
chapters.relation: Taking Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe seriously as a genocide story, the chapter reviews Lemkin's coinage and the 1948 Genocide Convention, then tests the mitigating factors - Deadpool's insanity, the X-Men's negligence in committing him to Psycho-Man's fake asylum, and Psycho-Man's manipulation - and finds none of them exculpatory. Killing Uatu the Watcher first and the Avengers next follows the genocide playbook of eliminating a community's intellectuals and pillars, and viewing his fellow characters as sheep completes the dehumanization that makes atrocity possible, while using everyone as means to his liberation violates Kant's demand never to treat persons as mere means. Invoking the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Thucydides' Melian Dialogue as the classic case of victims left unable to tell their story, the author concludes Deadpool bears full responsibility.

chapters.file: ch34 - VI. I’d Love to Get a Blow Job Why Existence Sucks.md
ch35 - 21. A Naughty Little Puppet, but Still a Puppet.md
chapters.relation: Deadpool's Killogy realization that the 'progenitors' puppeteer him becomes a tour of fatalism's three classic puppet masters: Aristotle's sea-battle argument from On Interpretation that truths about the future are already fixed, Augustine's problem of an all-knowing God whose foreknowledge (like Cullen Bunn's scripts) seems to cancel free choice, and the causal closure of the laws of nature, reinforced by Benjamin Libet's brain-activity experiments. Because cutting the strings of logic, God, or physics is impossible - 'you can hack away forever and never find the beginning . . . or the end' - the chapter concludes that the audience is no freer than Wade. The surviving Deadpool copes by embracing the absurdity of a scripted existence.

chapters.file: ch36 - 22. How to Solve the Contradictions in Deadpool Killustrated.md
chapters.relation: Because Deadpool Killustrated has him kill the real Captain Ahab, Ishmael both dies at Deadpool's hands and survives the Pequod's sinking in Moby-Dick, making the comic a depiction of something logically impossible in Hume's sense that contradictions cannot even be imagined. The chapter canvasses the escape routes: Matravers's claim that reading requires understanding rather than imagining, Gendler's aspect-imagining (Ahab as 'inspiration of Marvel heroes' rather than Melville's creation), Lewis's modal realism - defining the possible as what happens in some possible world, with the Killustrated Ahab a counterpart of Moby-Dick's and 'chunking' for contradictions - and finally Graham Priest's dialetheism and impossible worlds for stories like 'Wade's Impossible Day' with its square circle.

chapters.file: ch37 - 23. A Chimichanga for the Mercenary Soul.md
chapters.relation: Through Gramsci's Prison Notebooks the chapter casts Deadpool as the 'Eternal Proletariat': the military superstructure (Weapon X) recruited him precisely because he was broke and class-positioned, and as a mercenary he has no capital, no upward mobility, and no exit from wage-killing. His hunger beyond money - the Bullseye payday that ends in him shooting himself, the dead shark's verdict 'what you are . . . is alone' - drives him toward the X-Men, read as a subaltern coalition of the marginalized like Gramsci's socialist parties. But as a non-mutant 'mutate' who cannot meet the hegemonic standard of heroism (the Hit-Monkey arc with Spider-Man, his bitter plea to Wolverine that 'at least they wanted you'), his only Gramscian options are coalition building or reshaping the X-Men's culture from inside.

chapters.file: ch38 - 24. Won’t the Real Wade Wilson Please Stand Up.md
chapters.relation: Evil Deadpool, assembled from Wade's discarded body parts with all his old memories, makes Wade a walking Ship of Theseus, and the chapter runs the puzzle through Plutarch's original, Hobbes's reconstructed-ship variant, and Locke's Prince-and-Cobbler memory criterion, staged as a Thor/Thing body swap. Memory fails because Evil Deadpool shares Wade's memories, so the candidates become Schechtman's narrative and person-life views, Parfit's branching survival - neither is the original, and identity is not what matters anyway - and finally Unger's core-capacity view: Wade remains the real Deadpool by continuing to be a conscious being, while his detached parts ceased to be Deadpool parts the moment they were replaced.

chapters.file: ch39 - VII. Are You There, God It’s Me, Abandoned and All Alone in the Universe, You Stupid Mother- $ #($ %!.md
ch40 - 25. Deadpool Kills God.md
chapters.relation: The chapter declares Deadpool genuinely evil - shooting the defeated for fun, killing for money, then wiping out an entire universe - yet shifts the blame to the writers, the 'progenitors' who author every evil he commits and will not even let him think of escaping, making them the gods of the Marvel universe. By parity of reasoning it argues that if God created a world knowing every evil in it (Hitler, factory farms, tsunamis, SIDS), then all that evil is part of the plan and appealing to free will is blowing smoke. The author's real question is why anyone should obey a being who permits such suffering, dismissing do-as-he-says morality as cowardice before the lightning bolt: 'Go get him, Deadpool. Kick his bearded ass.'

chapters.file: ch41 - 26. Why We Love to Watch Deadpool . . . Play with Himself.md
chapters.relation: Using the Deadpool video game, the chapter argues Wade is a god who is all-powerful (rewriting the game world with his crayon-scrawled script and manufacturing fake credits), all-knowing (reading the player's mind through the fourth wall and literally entering Rogue's), and plainly not all-good (slapping an unconscious Wolverine, ogling dead Vertigo, ignoring Apocalypse three times for a billion dollars), so that dystheism - belief in a god with serious issues - dissolves the problem of evil. The free-will defense collapses because Deadpool wrote the script the villains obey, giving players only the illusion of choice. The voices in Wade's head are explicitly cast as Freud's structural model, with his Ego and SuperEgo talking while WadePrime, the Id, does most of the voice-work.

chapters.file: ch42 - 27. The Mystic with the Mouth.md
chapters.relation: In a lecture Deadpool keeps interrupting, the chapter reads the Merc's violence through Bataille's Theory of Religion: sacrifice as the search for lost intimacy, killing as the moment sacrificer and victim escape the profane world of mere things into sacred immanence, and sovereignty as the freedom glimpsed in destruction, with Rudolf Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans naming the awe Deadpool's massacres (the Circle Chase nunchuks, the Ultimate cartoon, the movie's highway slaughter) provoke. His 'dark Dao' of unhappy wandering is then set against the playful ways of the Zhuangzi - Cook Ding's ox-butchering, the Peng bird, the maimed teacher Wang Tai - as a Daoist path of inner-worldly transcendence that is amoral and gore-soaked. The payoff is the human tension of being both animal and angel: Deadpool is 'a savage god of mystical mayhem.'

chapters.file: ch43 - 28. Zen and the Art of Deadpool.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues Deadpool's unconventional style belies a Zen Buddhist disposition: created as a balance of Spider-Man's wit and Wolverine's lethality (against his disciplined template Deathstroke), he displays mushin, the no-mind calm of the trained martial artist under fire. His story is mapped onto the Four Noble Truths - dukkha in the suicidal depression over his incurable cancer scarring, samudaya in his attachment to belonging that he masks with jokes and loner behavior, nirodha in his ended relationships with Death and Siryn, and magga in shooting himself in the head at the end of Dark Reign as a perverse stilling of the mind. His fourth-wall awareness is read as piercing maya, the veil of illusion, an enlightenment no other Marvel character shares, though he remains 'not a good Buddhist' since he still wallows in ego and attachment.

holes.name: Post-Heroic Warfare
holes.what: Edward Luttwak's thesis that modern technology (drones, standoff missiles) removes personal risk from combat, creating an unbridgeable gap between combatants and ending heroic warfare.
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues Deadpool's healing factor is precisely such a technology, denying both him and everyone who fights him any chance to display courage.

holes.name: Human Rights (Universal Declaration)
holes.what: The post-WWII doctrine that all humans possess inalienable rights by virtue of species membership, codified in the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
holes.why: Chapter 20 condemns Deadpool's genocide of the Marvel Universe by the Declaration's standard that every person's inherent dignity must be recognized and can be violated but never voided.

holes.name: Law of Non-Contradiction
holes.what: The logical principle that nothing can both be and not be, or have and lack a property, in the same respect at the same time.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues Deadpool Killustrated violates it - Ahab is killed by both the whale and Deadpool - and surveys what such impossible fictions mean for logic and imagination.

holes.name: Georges Bataille
holes.what: French theorist whose Theory of Religion defines religion as the search for lost intimacy recovered through sacrifice, violence, and sovereignty.
holes.why: Chapter 27 reads Deadpool's killings as exactly the sacrificial violence that dissolves the profane world and opens onto sacred immanence in Bataille's sense.
